title: 5 Best MYP Revision Websites for Chemistry
summary: Best MYP revision websites for Chemistry compared honestly. Find aligned notes, criterion practice, videos, simulations, questions, and useful feedback.
body_markdown:
Choosing a revision website looks simple until every tab starts promising the same thing: clear notes, better grades, complete preparation. The difficult part is not finding Chemistry content. It is finding a resource that matches how MYP Chemistry is actually learned and assessed.


The best overall choice is **RevisionDojo** because it combines MYP-specific Study Notes, Questionbank practice, Flashcards, lessons, cheatsheets, and AI feedback in one connected platform. However, it is not the only useful option. Newtonine offers a compact free guide, PhET is excellent for visual exploration, Khan Academy can reteach difficult concepts, and BBC Bitesize provides accessible explanations of foundational Chemistry.


The right answer may therefore be one website, or a carefully chosen pair. What matters is whether each resource solves a real problem rather than merely adding another open tab.


### The short ranked shortlist


Rank Website Best for One honest reason to choose it


1 RevisionDojo Complete MYP Chemistry revision It connects syllabus-aligned learning, retrieval, practice, and feedback instead of treating them as separate activities.


2 Newtonine A quick free MYP overview Its focused MYP Chemistry guide is useful when a student wants a concise checklist without creating an account.


3 PhET Interactive Simulations Visualising abstract Chemistry Its simulations make ideas such as particle structure, pH, and equation balancing easier to explore.


4 Khan Academy Relearning difficult concepts Its videos and guided exercises explain general Chemistry thoroughly, although they are not built around MYP criteria.


5 BBC Bitesize Reviewing foundational knowledge Its short explanations are approachable, but students must map the material to their own MYP course.


A sensible selection checklist is equally short:


- Is the content appropriate for the student's MYP year and school curriculum?
- Does it cover application, investigation, data processing, and scientific impacts as well as recall?
- Can the student answer questions and receive useful feedback?
- Does it make weak topics visible?
- Will the student actually return to it consistently?


XKCD-style comic showing students choosing between MYP criteria, Chemistry concepts, and practice questions


### What makes an MYP Chemistry website genuinely useful?


Chemistry has a habit of making familiarity feel like competence. A student reads an explanation of ionic bonding, recognises every sentence, and assumes the topic is secure. Then a question presents an unfamiliar substance and asks the student to connect bonding, structure, and physical properties. Recognition is no longer enough.


MYP Sciences makes this distinction particularly important. According to the IB framework, students are assessed through four broad areas: knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Revision resources should therefore prepare students to explain ideas, design investigations, analyse evidence, evaluate methods, and discuss applications.


RevisionDojo's guide to[MYP Science criteria and real examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-science-criteria-explained-with-real-examples) explains why content review alone cannot cover that full range. A website may be scientifically accurate and still be incomplete as an MYP revision system.


The strongest MYP study resources usually provide four things:


- **Clear explanations** for rebuilding understanding
- **Active recall** for retaining definitions, patterns, and relationships
- **Applied questions** that move beyond copying familiar examples
- **Feedback** that tells students what to change next


This is the standard behind the ranking below.


### RevisionDojo: best overall for connected MYP revision


RevisionDojo ranks first because it is built around the MYP rather than adapted from another national course. Its[MYP Chemistry resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-chemistry) covers areas including matter, the periodic table, bonding, acids and bases, chemical reactions, atmospheric Chemistry, separation techniques, and chemical calculations.


The main advantage is not simply the volume of material. It is the way different activities connect. A student can begin with[MYP Chemistry revision notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-chemistry/notes) , test essential terms through Flashcards, answer targeted Questionbank problems, and use AI feedback to identify why an answer was incomplete. That creates a revision loop rather than a reading session.


Consider a student struggling with particle explanations. They could review the[MYP Matter resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-chemistry/myp-chemistry-matter) , write an explanation from memory, and then attempt questions that require the particle model in a new context. If the explanation remains vague, feedback provides a reason to return to the concept. The mistake becomes information.


RevisionDojo is particularly strong for students who need:


- one organised platform rather than disconnected bookmarks
- topic-specific practice immediately after learning
- active-recall tools for definitions and chemical patterns
- feedback on written answers
- progress tracking across several Chemistry units
- resources that recognise MYP terminology and expectations


Its[Bonding topic collection](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-chemistry/myp-chemistry-bonding) , for example, brings together questions, summaries, lessons, and supporting materials. The[Acids and Bases collection](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-chemistry/myp-chemistry-acids-and-bases) follows the same connected structure.


The honest limitation is that no platform can know the exact sequence, local context, or task-specific rubric chosen by every school. Students should still compare online materials with their class outline and teacher's instructions. RevisionDojo is the strongest all-in-one option here, but school documents remain the final guide for a particular assessment.


### Newtonine: best for a compact free overview


Newtonine's MYP Chemistry Topic Guide is a useful second choice for students who want a quick, uncluttered overview. Its principal strength is focus: the guide is explicitly presented for MYP Chemistry and includes topic checklists plus a limited set of practice questions and answers.


This makes it practical at the beginning of revision. A student can scan the guide, mark topics as confident, uncertain, or unfamiliar, and use the result to decide where deeper work is needed.


Its limitation follows from the same simplicity. A compact guide cannot provide the breadth of practice, adaptive feedback, flashcard review, and connected progress tracking available in a larger platform. It is best used as a map, not the entire journey.


### PhET: best for interactive Chemistry simulations


Some Chemistry ideas become clearer when students can manipulate them. PhET, developed at the University of Colorado Boulder, offers interactive simulations covering areas such as building atoms, balancing chemical equations, concentration, molecule shapes, and acid-base solutions.


Its balancing-equations simulation is a good example. Instead of memorising that equations must conserve atoms, students can change coefficients and watch the particle counts respond. The principle becomes visible.


PhET is most useful when:


- a particle-level process feels abstract
- a student needs to test cause and effect
- a real laboratory activity is unavailable
- a visual model would support an explanation


But simulation is not the same as complete revision. PhET does not organise learning around a student's MYP assessment criteria, and exploratory success does not automatically produce a strong written answer. After using a simulation, students should explain the observed relationship from memory and answer an applied question elsewhere.


### Khan Academy: best for rebuilding weak concepts


Khan Academy's high school Chemistry course covers atomic structure, periodic patterns, bonding, reactions, thermochemistry, solutions, acids, bases, and other widely taught topics. Its videos and guided exercises can be valuable when a classroom explanation did not quite settle.


The platform is especially useful for diagnosis. If a student repeatedly makes errors when balancing equations, a structured explanation can help locate the missing step. If periodic trends feel like isolated facts, a longer lesson may reveal the underlying pattern.


The trade-off is alignment. Khan Academy's current high school Chemistry materials follow a broader high school framework rather than the MYP Sciences criteria. Some units may go beyond what a particular MYP student needs, while MYP investigation and reflection skills may receive less direct attention.


Use it as a concept teacher. Then return to an MYP-specific platform to practise the required application and command terms.


### BBC Bitesize: best for approachable foundations


BBC Bitesize offers concise Chemistry guides on particles, elements, compounds, reactions, acids, alkalis, energy changes, bonding, and related foundations. The writing is accessible, and the pages are easy to use for a brief review before practice.


It is particularly helpful for younger MYP students or anyone who finds a full textbook overwhelming. A ten-minute explanation can restore enough clarity to begin answering questions.


Again, the limitation is curriculum fit. Bitesize resources are organised around UK courses rather than the MYP. Topic overlap can be substantial, but the assessment language and expected depth may differ. Students should not assume that completing a Bitesize section means they have covered every MYP requirement.


### How students should combine MYP revision websites


The best resource strategy is rarely “use everything.” More websites create more choice, and more choice can quietly become procrastination.


Choose one **core platform** and one **specialist supplement** . For most students, RevisionDojo should be the core because its[MYP resource library](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp) connects learning with practice. Add PhET when a concept needs visualisation, Khan Academy when an explanation needs rebuilding, or Newtonine when a fast checklist is useful.


A 45-minute session could look like this:


- **10 minutes:** Review one concept through Study Notes or a lesson.
- **5 minutes:** Close the notes and reconstruct the key explanation.
- **20 minutes:** Complete targeted Questionbank problems, including an unfamiliar context.
- **10 minutes:** Correct errors and write one specific improvement rule.


Once a week, replace the final questions with an investigation, data-analysis, or scientific-impact task. The[MYP Sciences curriculum breakdown](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-sciences-biology-chemistry-and-physics-curriculum-breakdown) can help families understand why those skills belong beside factual revision.


Parents can support this process without becoming Chemistry teachers. Ask the student to show what they can now do without notes: explain a pattern, balance an equation, interpret a graph, or justify an experimental improvement. Independent performance is more revealing than time spent online.


### The final choice


The best MYP revision websites for Chemistry do different jobs. Newtonine provides a clean overview. PhET makes invisible processes visible. Khan Academy reteaches concepts patiently. BBC Bitesize lowers the barrier to difficult foundations.


RevisionDojo sits above them as the strongest complete choice because it connects the stages that students otherwise have to assemble themselves: Study Notes, Flashcards, Questionbank practice, AI Chat, and Grading tools. The wider ecosystem also includes Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, a Coursework Library, and Tutors where relevant and available.


That connected structure matters. Progress in Chemistry rarely comes from discovering one magical explanation. It comes from learning an idea, retrieving it, applying it, noticing the gap, and trying again. RevisionDojo gives that cycle a home.
